topic: llama.cpp's ten-build morning and why your pinned tag is the whole game
title: llama.cpp moved ten builds today
description: On 02 Oct 2026 llama.cpp pushed ten nightly builds in one morning, three of them inside four hours and twenty-five minutes. Why your old binary rejects new GGUFs, what a pinned tag actually pins, and what to run tonight.
hook_text: Rebuild tonight: ten tagged builds this morning
hook_candidates: Rebuild tonight: ten llama.cpp builds this morning.
Re-pin tonight: ten llama.cpp builds shipped this morning.
Ten builds by breakfast, and your checkout is stale.
Your GGUF errors are one rebuild from gone tonight.
One tag tonight makes your llama.cpp reproducible.
Ten builds this morning; yours is months old.
Ten llama.cpp builds before lunch. Re-pin tonight.
llama.cpp has no stable release. Just nightlies.
You cloned llama.cpp once. It's been quietly rotting.
A maintainer dated your recent build to January.
narration_full: Rebuild tonight: ten tagged builds this morning. You built llama.cpp from source once and never updated. A release bot tagged ten builds before breakfast. Three landed within four hours and twenty-five minutes. Those b numbers are documented nightlies, automated development builds. The seven forty-two bus you board again tomorrow. Two builds can differ, not just schedules. Your old binary rejects new GGUF files, single-file model containers. The file is fine. The binary predates the architecture. The catch: a pinned commit pins code, not compiler or GPU flags. Builds target the hardware they see. Tonight, read the build line, fetch the tags, check out one exact nightly, rebuild. The GGUF that failed loads, and your setup is only as reproducible as the tag you write down.

analogy.mapping: a b-tag is the 7:42 bus you can board again tomorrow
analogy.limit: two builds can differ in behavior, not just schedule
